Good afternoon, Chairs Tipping and Roeder and the other distinguished members of the Joint
Standing Committee on Labor. I am Bill Brown, the Director of Actuarial and Legislative Affairs
for the Maine Public Employees Retirement System (MainePERS).
MainePERS is neither for nor against LD 2085. We are here to provide information and to offer
any assistance the Committee may request regarding this bill.

State employees are covered by either a "regular plan" or a "special plan." The majority of state
employees are covered by the regular plan, which permits retirement after twenty-five years of service and/or attainment of normal retirement age of 60, 62 or 65. Special plans typically allow for retirement with fewer years of service and/or at a younger age. Because of the more
'
favorable provisions of the special plans, they are more expensive to fund.

Most emergency communications positions at the Department of Public Safety are covered by
the 1998 Special Plan. PL 2021, c. 398, Pt. KKK moved emergency communications specialists,

specialist -- leads, specialist supervisors and dispatch system administrators to the special plan

as of July 1, 2020. As drafted, LD 2085 would move two additional positions from the regular

plan

to the

special

plan.
`

Under

this

plan,

participants

become

eligible

to

retire

in

one

of two

ways: 1) by accruing 25 years of service in a covered capacity; or 2) by accruing 10 years under

the 1998 Special Plan and attaining age 55. Under the first provision, all service in a covered

capacity is counted towards meeting the 25-year requirement while under the second provision,

only service earned in a covered capacity after the date that a specific group is included in the

plan is counted towards meeting the 10 year requirement.

There is no unfunded actuarial liability created by this bill because the employees in these positions were in other positions covered by the 1998 Special Plan as of the most recent
valuation. There would be an increase in normal costs and member contributions going
forward, but those are not required to be funded up front.

Representative Bunker and members of the Committee on Labor, I am Michael Labbe
Director of the Emergency Communications Bureau at the Department of Public Safety,
and appear before you today in support of LD 2085, An Act to Modify Service
Retirement Provisions to Include Additional Emergency Communications Positions in the 1998 Special Plan.

In July 2020 team members of Consildated Emergency Communications Bureau that possessed the titles of Emergency Communications Specialist, Emergency Communications Specialist Lead, Emergency Communications Specials Supervisor, and Emergency Dispatch Admin were give the option to join the 1998 Special Retirement plan, at that time the title Emergency Communications Director position was not
included.

The 1998 Special Plan requires 25 years of service with no minimum age restriction, or
10 years of service and age 55 to be eligible for a full retirement. The standard retirement
plan is 25 years of service AND age 65 (depending on start date) to be eligible for a full
retirement. Team members in the Emergency Communications Specialist categories
were granted access to the Special Plan because of the high stress nature of the work they perform. Our Emergency Communication team members are the vital link between the public and emergency services, gathering critical information, and dispatching

Before the Joint Standing Committee on Labor
Good afternoon, Senator Tipping, Representative Roeder and members of the Labor Committee.
I am Stephan Bunker and I represent House District 75, which includes the communities of
Farmington and Chesterville. I'm here today to introduce LD 2085, An Act to Modify Service
Retirement Provisions to Include Additional Emergency Communications Positions in the
1998 Special Plan.
In 1995, I was selected as Maine's first 911 Bureau Director and challenged with implementing the universal three-digit dial system. The steps included community addressing, coordinating with the many independent telcos, Geographic Information System (GIS) mapping and selecting modern call taking technology for the 911 centers. I then quickly realized the important, but
underappreciated, role that dispatchers play in the system.
I am proud to say that I was able to implement Maine's first training and certification standards
for dispatchers and developed a modern training lab at the police academy in Vassalboro, delivering a basic training curriculum to new hires. I later implemented the training standards for emergency medical dispatch, which gave dispatchers the skills to offer pre-arrival, life saving coaching to callers while the ambulance was in route. Maine was the first to implement the
standard statewide.
More recently, Maine added emergency fire dispatching standards to train dispatchers on how to
better handle fire and rescue calls, this again is also a statewide standard.
Where once, dispatchers were considered little more than glorified office workers, they are now becoming seen as true professionals and identified as the "FIRST" first responders alongside our
police, fire and ambulance personnel.
Dispatchers are now considering this work as a career. However, given the tremendous pressures that come with the work, it is a constant struggle to recruit and retain these essential workers. I feel that it is most important that we recognize their work with appropriate salary and benefits,
